correctness.rationale: Double-counting species groups contained in a sampled site subset yields F_r(k)=sum_{t>=k} binom(t,k)H_r(t); the alternating binomial transform inverts it for every finite N and r. The raw first two moments recover order-two factorial moments. Each witness distribution was enumerated explicitly. Ambiguity is impossible for at most two species or two sites by support-size and two-point arguments. At three sites and up to four species, the only same-sum/same-squares collision in [0,4] is (0,3,3) versus (1,1,4), ruled out by comparing the two-site samples; thus N+S=7 is the least combined size. Standalone exact checker verified 94,773 inversion instances, 2,800 small binary incidence matrices, 35 integer triple cases and both witnesses. All arbitrary-N claims rest on analytic identities, not finite extrapolation.

originality.rationale: The identified literature gives mean-zeta occupancy inversion, co-occurrence/covariance indices, and site-variance diagnostics. The new theorem uses factorial moments to reconstruct *aggregate intersection-size spectra* and pairs that representation with sharp two-axis and total-size thresholds for complete distributional nonidentification. The inverse transform is standard binomial inversion and is not claimed as invented; prior mean inversion can be reapplied to tuple-species, so residual prior coverage under this reduction is explicitly recognized. In the inspected full texts and matching research-record searches, the exact sharp third-order indistinguishability theorem and two minimal witnesses were not found.
residual_risks: Binomial-transform inversion is classical and may appear in earlier incidence/hypergraph design literature under a different name.
Some formula displays in the closest ecological primary sources are images, so textual comparison could miss a formula-equivalent appendix statement.
Independent novelty/importance assessment has not been performed; exact moments may be statistically unstable when estimated from data.

value.rationale: The object is a central incidence-based multi-site biodiversity statistic. In settings where full species-by-site matrices are lost or infeasible to retain, exact mean and variance zeta curves recover a naturally relevant full histogram of pairwise common-site extents, but leave higher-order structure unresolved. The theorem gives a complete all-order reconstruction mechanism and an exact smallest total community-size cutoff (seven species+sites), with sharp separate 3-site/5-species and 3-species/4-site witnesses; the latter show opposite skewness despite identical first-two-moment curves. It states a substantive information boundary, not just an identity or arbitrary table. Scope excludes inferential stability and causal interpretations.
